The Crow Indians traditionally claimed the area including the lease tracts as part of the Crow Country, by reason of discovery and intermittent occupancy since the early 1700's. The Fort Laramie Treaties of 1851 and 1858 gave legality to this claim by including the region as part of the 38 million acres of land described and assigned to Crow use and ownership.
Reservation History
The original 1851 Treaty of Laramie defined and set aside for the Crows a reservation of 38 million acres. An initial reduction to 9 million acres by the third Treaty of Laramie (in 1868) was followed by subsequent reductions, until today the Crow Reservation encompasses less than 2,300,000 acres.
The reservation headquarters or agency was moved to its present location in 1884 and the people moved to the eastern part of the diminishing reservation. At this time the Crows became much more familiar with the Tullock and Sarpy Creek country. Some families received land allotments in the Yellowstone valley and lived there, but none settled in the Sarpy Creek or Tullock Creek regions. The Crows living in the present Hardin area hunted deer and antelope there, and several families grazed their horse herds there.
